## keyframeBrowser.kt { #keyframebrowser-kt }

Reading a *collection* of saved keys the way [`KeyframeScope`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keyframescope) reads one: a glob of key files in,
a slot-major summary out.

### Why slot-major

A directory of keys is a sparse three-axis cube — file × version × slot — and only one of those
axes tells you anything you did not already know. You know your file names. What you cannot see
from a directory listing is which slots you actually kept pushing on, which have been frozen since
the first save, and which are missing from half the files because the scope grew a target after
they were written. So this pivots to slots, and every summary here is computed across files
rather than within one.

### What `load` reads

`load` decodes each matched file straight to [`KeyDTO`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt-keydto) rather than going through
[`KeyframeScope.loadKey`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--loadkey), which fills [`KeyframeScope.missingKey`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--missingkey) defaults for names a file lacks —
exactly right when you are about to apply a key and exactly wrong when you are trying to *see*
which names a file lacks. The browser wants the file as written.

Version history is read lazily. `load` calls [`KeyframeScope.keyVersions`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--keyversions) for each file, which
lists a directory and parses one manifest, but it does not open the numbered snapshots. Those are
only read when [`slotHistory`](visualization.md#keyframebrowser-kt--keyframecollection--slothistory) is asked for one slot's trajectory — a hundred saves of ten files is
a thousand files, and no one wants that on open.

### Failure is per-file

A collection with one unparseable file still browses. `load` records the failure in
[`KeyframeCollection.problems`](visualization.md#keyframebrowser-kt--keyframecollection--problems) and carries on, so one bad file does not make the other nine
invisible.

### SlotDisplay { #keyframebrowser-kt-slotdisplay }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">sealed</span> <span class="k">interface</span> <span class="nc">SlotDisplay</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/animation/keyframes/keyframeBrowser/#L655)

How a slot's spread should be drawn. The split is not cosmetic: it follows [`KeyframeScope.interpolate`](graphics.md#keyframer-kt--keyframescope--interpolate), which blends numbers and vectors and *steps* strings, StackSL source and source blocks. A slot that steps has no range, only a set of variants, and drawing a bar for one would claim a continuum that does not exist.

## LorisVisualizer.kt { #lorisvisualizer-kt }

Draws a [`LorisModel`](audio.md#loris-kt-lorismodel)'s partial trajectories as an interactive HTML panel next to its waveform.

[`visualizationHtml`](visualization.md#lorisvisualizer-kt--visualizationhtml) plots each partial's breakpoints at their real times on a cents, ERB or Hz axis
([`LorisFrequencyAxis`](visualization.md#lorisvisualizer-kt-lorisfrequencyaxis)), shares the time window, cursor and click-to-seek with the waveform view, and
caps how many partials and points are drawn ([`LorisViewOptions`](visualization.md#lorisvisualizer-kt-lorisviewoptions)). The caps affect drawing only.

## interactionnets.kt { #interactionnets-kt }

Interaction nets as a live-codeable medium: a graph whose nodes rewrite each other wherever two of them
touch principal port to principal port, with a DSL for building nets, a rule language for the rewrites, a
scheduler that decides which collision fires next, and a force-directed layout so you can watch it happen.

Start at [`net`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt--net) to build one, [`rules`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt--rules) to say how it rewrites, [`Reducer`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-reducer) to run it, and [`Net.toFLines`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt--net--toflines) or
[`Box.showInteractionNet`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt--showinteractionnet) to look at it. [`Lambda`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-lambda) is a ready-made vocabulary (APP, LAM, DUP, ERASE, ROOT,
VAR, CONST) with its own rule book, if you want the classical behaviour rather than your own.

A compact, single-file interaction-net playground meant to be easy to lift into a larger codebase,
but also meant to be a fertile computational substrate for live coding art.

What is in here:
- a small in-memory interaction-net graph model
- a Kotlin DSL for building whole nets and reusable graph fragments
- two rewrite styles:
    1) a declarative "automatic rewiring" DSL built around ext(side, aux)
    2) an escape hatch for arbitrary custom rewrites in ordinary Kotlin
- configurable active-pair scheduling
- a simple force-directed layout with incremental seeding of rewrite RHS nodes at the LHS center
- FLine/output rendering plus SVG export for quick inspection
- a small lambda-oriented bundle including APP, LAM, DUP, ERASE, ROOT, VAR, CONST

Design intent:
- Keep the core tiny and hackable.
- Make the common case pleasant without removing low-level control.
- Be explicit about where the model is still incomplete.
- Treat the system less like a theorem prover and more like a graph chemistry / reactive medium.

The artistic framing:
This file is not most interesting as a route to "real lambda calculus". It is more interesting as a
local, spatial, rewiring-based substrate for live coding. In that framing:

- principal ports are not just logical redex triggers; they are collision points, activation sites,
  rhythmic contact surfaces
- auxiliary ports are not just variables; they can be treated as tension channels, color buses,
  growth directions, continuation hooks, memory strands, or signal paths
- rewrite rules are not merely reductions; they are local laws of motion, branching, fusion,
  mutation, decay, reflection, gating, or pulse propagation
- active-pair scheduling is not merely evaluation order; it is rhythm, phrasing, emphasis, groove,
  cascade control
- layout is not merely display; it is motion memory and can become part of the meaning of the system

DUP and ERASE in this context:
DUP and ERASE are useful here less as strict lambda-calculus machinery and more as artistic growth and
decay primitives.

- DUP can mean branching, echo, motif propagation, splitting a line of force into two descendants,
  or generating two related but diverging futures
- ERASE can mean fade, pruning, absorption, dissipation, culling, or a sink that removes pressure from
  a local region

In a more expressive live system, DUP does not need to be perfectly literal duplication. It can create
two descendants with slight positional offsets, inherited state, hue drift, phase drift, timing skew,
energy split, or generation markers. Likewise ERASE does not need to be instantaneous deletion; it can
become gradual attenuation, shrinkage, or multi-frame disappearance.

Why this is promising for live coding art:
- Local causality: every visible change comes from a small neighborhood interaction.
- Spatial meaning: the graph is data and choreography at once.
- Compositionality: a small table of rewrite laws can yield rich large-scale behavior.
- Performability: rules, scheduler, layout constants, render mapping, and node injection can all be
  changed while the system is running.

Activation order as an instrument:
Reduction order is a first-class artistic control. A deterministic scheduler can feel mechanical;
randomized scheduling can shimmer; energy-biased or cursor-biased scheduling can create bursts,
avalanches, attraction, or spotlighting. Treat scheduling as part of the score.

Layout as part of computation:
The incremental layout already gives new RHS nodes a positional memory by seeding them at the centroid
of the consumed active pair before relaxation. That idea can be pushed further. Rewrite rules can read
or influence geometry; branch direction can depend on current edge angle; replication distance can
depend on energy; eligibility can depend on local spatial conditions; layout velocity can feed rendering
or sound. The graph need not be computed first and visualized second.

A "wet" semantics is often better than a perfectly dry one:
For artistic purposes, clean instantaneous replacement is sometimes less interesting than sticky,
physicalized replacement. Newly created nodes can inherit centroid and velocity. Consumed edges can
leave ghosts. Erased nodes can decay over a few frames. Duplicated nodes can repel strongly at birth
and then settle. Rules can emit transient sparks or decorative residues. These choices improve visual
legibility and expressiveness during rapid change.

The next high-leverage extension is per-node state:
Adding a small mutable state record to each node would make the substrate much richer. Examples:

    data class State(
        var energy: Double = 1.0,
        var phase: Double = 0.0,
        var hue: Double = 0.0,
        var age: Double = 0.0
    )

Then rewrite rules can split energy on DUP, accumulate age, drift hue, mutate phase, and directly map
these quantities to radius, stroke weight, opacity, curvature, synthesis parameters, or triggering.

Rendering and sound hooks:
A rewrite can be more than a topology update. In a live system it is natural for a rewrite to also emit
events such as "flash this edge", "trigger a note", "spawn a particle", "increase camera pull", or
"mark this component active". That turns graph rewriting into the event engine for an audiovisual system.

Useful node archetypes for an artistic palette:
- Pulse   : propagates motion or activation
- DUP     : bifurcates structure or motive
- ERASE   : consumes / attenuates / prunes
- Delay   : holds activity for N frames or beats
- Gate    : conditionally passes or blocks interaction
- Mirror  : swaps neighborhoods / reflects flow
- Fuse    : merges strands
- Noise   : injects stochastic variation
- Anchor  : spatial stabilizer
- Bloom   : expands into decorative local structure

A note on rigor:
This file adds DUP and ERASE agents in the usual explicit-resource spirit, but it is not trying to be a
complete optimal reducer. There is no full fan/fan commuting story, no full lambda frontend, and no
claim of theoretical completeness. That is deliberate. The value here is as a hackable medium with:

- topology that changes
- space that remembers
- order that matters
- small laws that create style

In other words: treat this as a graph chemistry for live coding.

### LayoutConfig { #interactionnets-kt-layoutconfig }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">LayoutConfig</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">repulsion</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">2500.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">springLength</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">90.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">springStrength</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.015</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">damping</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.82</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">timeStep</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">jitter</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">8.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">clampStep</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">20.0</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/data/graph/interactionnets/#L259)

The knobs on the force-directed layout that [`Net.relax`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt--net--relax) runs — every node pushing every other apart, every edge pulling its two ends together.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <a id="interactionnets-kt--layoutconfig--repulsion"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">repulsion</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | How hard every node pushes every other away. Falls off as `1/d²`, so it sets the empty space between unconnected nodes without much affecting connected ones. |
| <a id="interactionnets-kt--layoutconfig--springlength"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">springLength</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | The distance an edge is happy at, in position units. The quickest single knob for the overall scale of the picture. |
| <a id="interactionnets-kt--layoutconfig--springstrength"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">springStrength</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | How strongly an edge pulls back toward [`springLength`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt--layoutconfig--springlength). Large values make the net rigid and jittery. |
| <a id="interactionnets-kt--layoutconfig--damping"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">damping</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Velocity retained per step. Below 1 is what makes the simulation settle at all; toward 1 it wobbles for far longer, and at 1 it never stops. |
| <a id="interactionnets-kt--layoutconfig--timestep"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">timeStep</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Integration step. Scales both the velocity update and the movement, so raising it is a faster but less stable simulation. |
| <a id="interactionnets-kt--layoutconfig--jitter"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">jitter</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Stored but **unused** by the current layout step — new nodes get their initial scatter from [`Net.create`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt--net--create) instead. |
| <a id="interactionnets-kt--layoutconfig--clampstep"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">clampStep</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Per-step speed limit, in position units. What stops two nearly coincident nodes from firing each other off the canvas. |

### NodeState { #interactionnets-kt-nodestate }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">NodeState</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">energy</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">phase</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">hue</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">age</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">scalars</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MutableMap</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">&gt;</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">linkedMapOf</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/data/graph/interactionnets/#L297)

The mutable per-node payload that turns a bare interaction net into something worth watching: four named quantities the renderer already reads, plus [`scalars`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt--nodestate--scalars) for anything else you want to carry.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <a id="interactionnets-kt--nodestate--energy"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">energy</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Drives node radius when drawn, and is what the energy-biased [`PairSelectors`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-pairselectors) rank pairs by. Every operation here floors it at 0, but nothing caps it. |
| <a id="interactionnets-kt--nodestate--phase"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">phase</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Carried and split, but **nothing in this file interprets it** — yours to use, though the renderer does fall back to it for a node's port angle when the node has no connected neighbours. |
| <a id="interactionnets-kt--nodestate--hue"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">hue</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Drives colour, as a fraction of a turn. Wrapped at render time rather than here, so it may drift far outside `0..1` and that is fine. |
| <a id="interactionnets-kt--nodestate--age"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">var</span> <span class="n">age</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code> | Advanced only by [`Net.incrementAges`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt--net--incrementages), in whatever unit you pass it — so age runs on the clock you choose. Nudges drawn lightness. |
| <a id="interactionnets-kt--nodestate--scalars"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">scalars</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MutableMap</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | Room for your own named quantities. Deep-copied by [`copyDeep`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt--nodestate--copydeep) and blended key-wise by `blend`, where a key missing from one side counts as 0. |
| <a id="interactionnets-kt--nodestate--copydeep"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">copyDeep</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">NodeState</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/data/graph/interactionnets/#L315) | An independent copy, [`scalars`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt--nodestate--scalars) map included, so later mutation of either cannot reach the other. |
| <a id="interactionnets-kt--nodestate--evolved"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">evolved</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">energyScale</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">energyBias</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">phaseShift</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">hueShift</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">ageDelta</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">NodeState</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/data/graph/interactionnets/#L330) | A copy with the four quantities moved on — the "one node becomes one node, a little different" step for a rewrite rule to hand its replacement. |
| <a id="interactionnets-kt--nodestate--split"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">split</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">parts</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">branch</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">attenuation</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">hueSpread</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">phaseSpread</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">ageDelta</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">NodeState</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/data/graph/interactionnets/#L353) | One branch's share of this state when a node divides into `parts` — the state side of a DUP-style rewrite. |

### Port { #interactionnets-kt-port }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">Port</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">node</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Node</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">index</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">kind</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">PortKind</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/data/graph/interactionnets/#L433)

One port on one node — the thing edges connect. Port 0 is always the principal port and `1..auxPorts` the auxiliaries, which is why [`Node.aux`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt--node--aux) takes a 0-based index and adds one for you.

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">RewriteEvent</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">kind</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">at</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Vec2</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">magnitude</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">data</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Map</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">&gt;</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">emptyMap</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/data/graph/interactionnets/#L1469)

| <a id="interactionnets-kt--rewriteevent--data"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">data</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Map</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code> | Any extra named numbers the rule wanted to pass along. Copied on emit, so the map you passed is not retained. |

### ActivationOrder { #interactionnets-kt-activationorder }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">ActivationOrder</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/data/graph/interactionnets/#L1881)

The ready-made choices for *which* of several possible reactions fires next — reduction order as a dial.

## lambdaterms.kt { #lambdaterms-kt }

λ-terms as a front end to the interaction nets in `interactionnets.kt`: text in, a reduced net out, a term back.

The shortest useful thing is `LambdaTerms.normalise`, which runs parse, compile, reduce and readback in one call:

    val run = LambdaTerms.normalise("(\\m n f x. m f (n f x)) (\\f x. f x) (\\f x. f (f x))")
    run.printed   // "λa. λb. a (a (a b))", Church three, from add one two
    run.steps     // how many reactions it took

Two public names sit behind that. [`Term`](visualization.md#lambdaterms-kt-term) is the syntax tree, with `Var`, `Lam` and `App` nested inside it so that
`Term.Lam("x", Term.Var("x"))` reads as what it is and none of the three short names leaks into `afield.lang.lambda`.
[`LambdaTerms`](visualization.md#lambdaterms-kt-lambdaterms) is everything done to one: parsing, printing, compilation to the [`Lambda`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-lambda) agent vocabulary, readback,
and the reference evaluator the net's answer is checked against.

Every answer here is computed twice. The net is one route; `LambdaTerms.referenceNormalOrder` is the other, and
reduces by capture-avoiding substitution with no nets and no sharing anywhere in it, so the two routes share no
machinery beyond the term type. `LambdaTerms.corpus` is the set of closed terms both are run over.

The file lands on the Visualization page because a finished run keeps the [`Net`](visualization.md#interactionnets-kt-net) it reduced, and `Net.toFLines`
draws that net with its active pairs emphasised.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/lang/lambda/lambdaterms.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/lang/lambda/lambdaterms/)

## PetriAnalysis.kt { #petrianalysis-kt }

What a net can tell you about itself without being played: how long it is, and whether it is
about to wedge.

Petri nets come with about fifty years of theory attached, and much of it answers questions a live
coder actually has. Two of them are worth the code.

**"How long is this?"** A *T-invariant* is a bag of firings that returns the net to the marking it
started from, which is precisely a loop, and a net's minimal T-invariants are its natural musical
periods. A net built from a five-step ring against a three-step ring has two of them, of five
firings and three, and how long the whole net takes to come back round is a separate question:
fifteen steps here, which [`PetriRun.lasso`](visualization.md#petrinets-kt--petrirun--lasso) finds by running it. [`tInvariants`](visualization.md#petrianalysis-kt--tinvariants) answers the
structural question from the incidence matrix alone, with no notion of time or of the initial
marking; [`PetriNet.checkLoopIsInvariant`](visualization.md#petrianalysis-kt--checkloopisinvariant) asserts that the loop the engine actually ran is itself a
T-invariant (a combination of the minimal ones, in the polyrhythm case), so when it fails the
engine and the algebra disagree and one of them has a bug.

**"Is this about to wedge?"** A net that starves is silent, and finding out at the wrong moment is
what makes live coding frightening. [`willDeadlock`](visualization.md#petrianalysis-kt--willdeadlock) runs the net forward and tells you before you
commit the change. For the stronger question — whether *any* interleaving can wedge, rather than
the one this net's conflict policy chose — see `PetriStateSpace.kt`.

### Limits

- Invariants are structural. They see arc weights and nothing else: **inhibitor and read arcs are
  invisible to them**, because neither changes the marking and the incidence matrix is a record of
  change. A net whose behaviour turns on an inhibitor arc has invariants that describe a net it is
  not. [`usesTestArcs`](visualization.md#petrianalysis-kt--usestestarcs) is how you find out, and [`report`](visualization.md#petrianalysis-kt--report) says so itself.

- Recurrence is detected on [`PetriMarking.signature`](visualization.md#petrinets-kt--petrimarking--signature), which compares colours by equality: a net
  that swaps one pattern for another has changed, and one that brings the same pattern object
  round again has recurred. A net that makes a *new* colour on every firing never recurs.

- Everything here is bounded. A net with an unbounded place has infinitely many markings and no
  loop to find; the answer is null rather than a hang.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/petri/PetriAnalysis.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/petri/PetriAnalysis/)

**Used in:** [Petri nets](../petri_nets.md), [Petri notation cheatsheet](../petri_cheatsheet.md), [Agent transcript gallery](../agent_transcripts.md)

## PetriNets.kt { #petrinets-kt }

Petri nets: places hold tokens, transitions move them, and the whole thing is a clock. This file
is the model and the engine, and the types the rest of the layer is a view onto.

It knows nothing about music. The one thing it takes from `afield.audio.synth` is [`PatQ`](patterns.md#tidalpatterns-kt-patq), the
exact rational Field uses for time everywhere. `PetriMusic.kt` turns a net into a `PatPattern`,
`PetriVisual.kt` draws one, `PetriNotation.kt` parses the `#petri` text form, and
`PetriStateSpace.kt` and `PetriAnalysis.kt` answer questions about one.

Read the surface from the outside in. Build a net: places are auto-declared on first mention, so
a two-transition loop is three calls.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val net = petri {
    place("kick", tokens = 1)
    t("hit",  dur = cyc(1, 16), emit = "bd") { from("kick"); to("hats") }
    t("back", dur = cyc(1, 16), emit = "sd") { from("hats"); to("kick") }
}
```

Run it. A [`PetriRun`](visualization.md#petrinets-kt-petrirun) is a memoised, append-only trajectory: ask it for any instant and it replays
deterministically up to there.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
net.run().stepsUntil(PatQ.of(4)).flatMap { it.firings }.forEach(::println)
```

Tokens carry colour, and a colour can be anything: a note number, a sample name, a whole
`PatPattern`. That is what makes a net a song structure rather than a drum machine. Colours are
carried through a firing by default, so the pattern held in `verse` below is the colour of the
token that reaches `chorus`, with no lambda anywhere.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
place("verse", pat("bd*4"))          // one token whose colour is a pattern
t("build", dur = cyc(4)) { from("verse"); from("hats"); to("chorus") }
```

### Three timings, and why

- `PetriTiming.STEP` — **maximal step**. Every transition that is enabled at a grid tick fires,
  all against the marking as it stood at the start of the tick, and produced tokens do not
  become available until the tick is over. This is the drum-machine semantics, and the same
  synchronous step `BooleanNetworkSequencing.kt` sequences. Conflicts (two transitions wanting
  the same token) are resolved greedily in [`PetriConflict`](visualization.md#petrinets-kt-petriconflict) order.

- `PetriTiming.EVENT` — one transition per tick, the first in conflict order. Interleaving
  semantics; useful when you want a net to *walk* rather than pulse.

- `PetriTiming.TIMED` — firing takes time. A transition consumes its inputs at the instant it
  starts and produces its outputs `duration` later, so a token can be *in flight*, and a
  transition with `dur = cyc(4)` holds a four-cycle section open. Time advances to the next
  instant at which something happens, not on a grid.

In STEP and EVENT, `duration` does not affect token flow at all; it only sets how long the
emitted event lasts. In all three, `delay` shifts the emitted event and nothing else, so you can
nudge a hit late without perturbing the net's logic.

### Why the trajectory is reproducible

`PetriMusic.kt` presents a net as a `PatPattern`, and a `PatPattern` has to be a *pure function of
time*: the scheduler queries it cycle by cycle and every combinator in the language is free to
query it again, out of order. That only works if the trajectory is reproducible, so

- tokens are consumed FIFO, oldest first, never "some matching token";
- `PetriConflict.RANDOM` hashes `(seed, step index, transition name)` rather than pulling from a
  stateful RNG, so the answer does not depend on how many times anything was asked;
- [`PetriRun`](visualization.md#petrinets-kt-petrirun) memoises, so replay is not merely reproducible but literally the same objects.

A net whose conflict policy is genuinely non-deterministic cannot be presented as a pattern at
all. `PetriLive` performs one directly instead, rebuilding the run from the current marking
whenever you interfere with it.

## PetriNotation.kt { #petrinotation-kt }

The `#petri` text notation: a net you can retype while it is playing.

The Kotlin DSL in `PetriNets.kt` is the complete surface; anything you can express, you can
express there, including arbitrary lambdas. This file is the *terse* surface. Live coding is
editing, and editing a net is only pleasant when the whole net fits in view and one arc is one
line. For players, the whole notation is summarised on the
[Petri notation cheatsheet](../petri_cheatsheet.md).

```diffstatic {data-lang=petri}
#petri
!grid 1/16

kick : 1
kick -[ hit  @1/16 : bd ]-> hats
hats -[ back @1/16 : sd ]-> kick
```

[`petri`](visualization.md#petrinotation-kt--petri) turns that text into a `PetriNet`; [`petriParse`](visualization.md#petrinotation-kt--petriparse) returns the net along with everything it
has to say about the source.

### One line, one arc

```diffstatic {data-lang=petri}
pre -[ name @dur key=value : emit => combinator ]-> post
```

Both sides are `+`-joined lists of `weight*place`, and either may be empty: `-[ spawn ]-> p` is a
source and `p -[ sink ]->` is a drain. A place is created the first time it is mentioned. A
transition **may be named on more than one line**, which is how one with several inputs stays
readable; its settings belong on the first of those lines, and a later line's are ignored with a
warning.

```diffstatic {data-lang=petri}
verse  -[ build ]-> chorus
energy -[ build ]-> chorus
```

Prefixes on an input mark the two arcs that are not ordinary.

```diffstatic {data-lang=petri}
~armed  -[ fill ]-> hats        // inhibitor: only while armed is empty
&clock  -[ tick ]-> bar         // read/test: needs a token, consumes none
2*hats  -[ roll ]-> fill        // weight: needs two
```

### Place declarations

```diffstatic {data-lang=petri}
kick   : 1              // one black token
dst    : 0 ^4           // empty, and bounded at four
verse  : "bd ~ sd ~"    // ONE token whose colour is that pattern — a section
label  : 'lead'         // one token coloured with the literal string
notes  : #60, #64, #67  // three numeric tokens
```

The two kinds of quote differ: a double-quoted string is parsed as a *pattern* and a
single-quoted one stays a string, because a place holding a rhythm is what makes a net a song
structure rather than a drum machine.

### Directives

```diffstatic {data-lang=petri}
!timing step | event | timed
!grid 1/16
!conflict order | priority | round-robin | random
!seed 7
```

### Everything else

`//` starts a comment. A leading `#petri` line is the editor's marker and is ignored here. Colour
transforms after `=>` come from [`PetriCombinators`](visualization.md#petrinotation-kt-petricombinators), a fixed vocabulary rather than compiled
Kotlin, which keeps the notation quick to parse and the cheatsheet finite. When you want a real
lambda, that is what the Kotlin DSL is for.

Errors are collected rather than thrown at the first one: [`petriParse`](visualization.md#petrinotation-kt--petriparse) hands back everything it
found, so an editor can underline all of it at once. [`petri`](visualization.md#petrinotation-kt--petri) is the throwing convenience on top.

## PetriStateSpace.kt { #petristatespace-kt }

Every marking a net can reach by *any* interleaving, and the classical properties read off that:
boundedness, safety, deadlock, quasi-liveness, liveness, reversibility, home markings, mutual
exclusion. Exactly, and with a counterexample when the answer is no.

`PetriAnalysis.kt` asks the *deterministic* question instead: [`willDeadlock`](visualization.md#petrianalysis-kt--willdeadlock) runs the net forward
under its own [`PetriConflict`](visualization.md#petrinets-kt-petriconflict) policy and reports whether *that one* interleaving wedged, and
[`deadTransitions`](visualization.md#petrianalysis-kt--deadtransitions) calls a transition dead when it did not fire in *that one* run. For a live
coder that is usually the useful question, because the conflict policy is part of the instrument.

It is not the question the textbook asks, and not the one a five-philosopher table asks either. A
symmetric dining table deadlocks under some interleavings and not others, so running it once and
finding it still going proves nothing; you have to enumerate. That example is worked through under
[Checking every possible order](../petri_nets.md#checking-every-possible-order).

### A positive answer is sound; a negative answer needs a complete search

A deadlock the search *found* is real whether or not the budget ran out: it came with a firing
sequence, and [`PetriTrace.verify`](visualization.md#petristatespace-kt--petritrace--verify) re-fires that sequence through the engine to prove it. But
"there is no deadlock" is a claim about markings nobody visited, so every accessor that would make
such a claim returns `null`, meaning unknown, when the search was truncated
(`PetriSearchOutcome.BUDGET` rather than `PetriSearchOutcome.COMPLETE`). Nothing here reports a
truncated search as safe.

### What this sees that the incidence matrix cannot

The successor relation is [`PetriNet.fire`](visualization.md#petristatespace-kt--fire), which calls the engine's own binding step. So **read
arcs, inhibitor arcs, colour guards, `enabledIf` and place capacities are all handled**: an
explicit search asks "is this transition enabled here?" and gets the real answer, where
`tInvariants` and `pInvariants` ask the incidence matrix, which is a record of *change* and so
blind to every arc that does not move a token. A net whose mutual exclusion is enforced by an
inhibitor arc has no P-invariant that proves it, and a state space that does.

The price is the classical one: reachability for a net with inhibitor arcs is undecidable in
general, so this may exhaust its budget where the algebra would have answered instantly. The two
layers are complements, not replacements.

### Two searches, and when to use which

- [`PetriNet.stateSpace`](visualization.md#petristatespace-kt--statespace) is exact and handles every feature of the model, but only terminates on a
  bounded net. An unbounded one exhausts the budget and says so.
- [`PetriNet.coverability`](visualization.md#petristatespace-kt--coverability) is Karp–Miller: it accelerates growth to ω and therefore *always*
  terminates, which is how you get per-place boundedness for a net whose state space is infinite.
  Karp–Miller is only valid for plain place/transition nets, though. Inhibitor arcs, place
  capacities and colour-dependent behaviour each break the acceleration argument, and each adds
  an entry to [`PetriCoverabilityGraph.caveats`](visualization.md#petristatespace-kt--petricoverabilitygraph--caveats) rather than being dropped silently.

### The state key

[`PetriMarking.signature`](visualization.md#petrinets-kt--petrimarking--signature) is the obvious key and the wrong one here: it *sorts* the colours within
a place, so it loses arrival order, and consumption is FIFO, so two markings holding the same
multiset in a different order have genuinely different futures.

That makes the key **coarser** than the state, and a coarse key in a reachability search merges
states whose futures differ, which can hide a reachable deadlock behind an already-visited
marking and call the net safe. An unsound *safe* is the error that matters, so the key here is
strict: places, and the colours in them **in arrival order**, compared by the colours' own
`equals`.

The cost lands in the survivable direction. A net that mints a fresh colour object per firing has
an effectively infinite state space and exhausts the budget, and `PetriSearchOutcome.BUDGET`
reports that rather than guessing.

`PetriToken.born` is not in the key. The search fires everything at `PatQ.ZERO` — these are the
*untimed* semantics, with timing, grid and conflict policy all discarded — so `born` never varies
during a search anyway. The residual exposure is a guard or an `enabledIf` that reads `born`,
which the state space evaluates at zero and a real run does not.

## PetriVisual.kt { #petrivisual-kt }

Draws a Petri net as an `FLine` picture, and lets you click it to add tokens and fire transitions.

A Petri net has a standard picture: circles hold tokens, bars move them, arrows say where. The two
things you most need to see while debugging a net are which transitions are ready to go and where
the tokens are, so the drawing shows four things the plain graph does not:

- a **place** is a circle with its tokens as dots inside it, and a token carrying a `PatPattern`
  gets a ring rather than a dot, because a place holding a rhythm is a different kind of thing
  from a place holding a count;
- a **transition** is a bar, drawn dim when it cannot fire, bright when it is enabled, and filled
  when it is firing at the instant being drawn;
- an **inhibitor arc** ends in a small circle and a **read arc** in no head at all, the standard
  notation for a distinction a token count cannot show;
- **arc weights** above one are written on the arc.

Interaction goes through `FLine.onClick`, so it only works in the interactive outputs. Click a
place to drop a token in, click a transition to make it fire. Both need somewhere for the change to
go, so both are wired to a [`PetriLive`](audio.md#petrimusic-kt-petrilive); a [`PetriRun`](visualization.md#petrinets-kt-petrirun) is an immutable trajectory, and clicking one
only reports on it.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val live = net.live()
box.showPetriNet(live)          // click the picture; the net changes under your hands
```

### Layout

`PetriLayout.RING` draws a cycle as a cycle, which is what most drum nets are, and is chosen
automatically when the net is one. Otherwise `PetriLayout.FORCE` relaxes a spring model.
`PetriLayout.TALA` hands the net to d2's diagram layout engine instead, if you have built the
optional helper for it; it falls back to `PetriLayout.FORCE` if you have not.
[`PetriDrawing.at`](visualization.md#petrivisual-kt--petridrawing--at) pins anything you would rather place yourself.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/simulation/petri/PetriVisual.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/simulation/petri/PetriVisual/)

**Used in:** [Petri nets](../petri_nets.md), [Petri notation cheatsheet](../petri_cheatsheet.md)

## ControlLaw.kt { #controllaw-kt }

The mapping between a slider's travel and its value: linear, logarithmic, power-taper or bipolar.

[`ControlLaw`](visualization.md#controllaw-kt-controllaw) names the law and its wire spelling, [`ControlLawSpec`](visualization.md#controllaw-kt-controllawspec) pairs it with a range and maps
travel to value and back, and [`controlLawDecimals`](visualization.md#controllaw-kt--controllawdecimals) picks how many decimals a readout shows. The
`slider(...)` builder in the output controls takes a `law` argument of this type.

## canvasFlight.kt { #canvasflight-kt }

Filming Field: [`canvasFlight`](visualization.md#canvasflight-kt--canvasflight) flies the canvas through a document's bookmarks, live or to an MP4.

The flight opens on the first bookmark and holds, then flies to each next one and holds there. Each
leg eases in and out, zooming in log space while the point at the centre of the window travels in a
straight line across the canvas. Every three.js view showing on the canvas turns slowly about its own
target meanwhile, and gets its camera back afterwards.

Live, the flight runs in every window open on the document, on the browser's own clock. Filmed
(`record = "flight.mp4"`), it is rendered frame by frame in the capture page and encoded with
ffmpeg: the clock waits for each frame, so the film is smooth however long a frame takes.

The arithmetic is `afield.app.canvas.CanvasFlightTimeline`; the browser side is
`CanvasFlightClient`; the recorder is `afield.tools.docs.recordCanvasFlight`. Docs:
`public/docs/filming_the_canvas.md`.

## BoxLayout.kt { #boxlayout-kt }

"Lay out selection" — arranging boxes on the canvas the way a diagram tool would, using the
layout engines in `native/field-d2-layout`.

A document's boxes and the execution edges between them are a node-link diagram that happens to
be editable, so the same engine that draws a Petri net can tidy one. What makes this different
from drawing a Petri net is that the positions here are the user's: they were placed by hand,
they persist, and they are what the document looks like when it is opened again. So this only
ever runs when asked, only over what was asked for, and every move goes through
[`OperationTranscript.recordMove`](workspace.md#operation-transcript-kt--operationtranscript--recordmove) so one undo puts everything back.

Unlike `afield.simulation.petri.PetriLayout.TALA` there is no fallback: Field has no second box-layout
engine to drop to, so an absent helper is reported to the user rather than absorbed.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/layout/BoxLayout.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/layout/BoxLayout/)

## D2Layout.kt { #d2layout-kt }

Field's client for the `native/field-d2-layout` helper — d2's layout engines, TALA in
particular, over a one-shot subprocess.

**The helper is optional and this class is built around that.** Field does not build it, no
Gradle task references it, and it is absent in a fresh checkout. Every entry point here answers
`null` rather than throwing when the binary is missing, is the wrong protocol, times out, or
reports an error, and callers are expected to fall back to whatever they did before rather than
surface a failure. See `native/field-d2-layout/README.md` for the build, the wire format, and
why this is a subprocess and not a wasm module hosted in-process like libfaust.

One process per call. That looks profligate and is not: the helper starts in low single-digit
milliseconds against layouts that cost hundreds, so spawning is lost in the noise, and a
short-lived process means no state to corrupt and nothing to reap if Field exits mid-layout.
Repeated identical requests are served from [`cache`](workspace.md#importhelp-kt--cache) instead, which is what actually matters —
a Petri animation redraws the same net many times.

## alignment.kt { #alignment-kt }

Geometric tidying of box frames on the canvas: aligning, snapping and connection-guided
routing over a list of `Rect`s, plus the palette actions that apply them to a selection.

Three entry points, each taking rectangles and returning new ones in the same order:

- [`alignAndDistribute`](visualization.md#alignment-kt--alignanddistribute) lines the rectangles up in bands, vertically or horizontally
  ([`Orientation`](visualization.md#alignment-kt-orientation)), spaced by [`LayoutParams`](visualization.md#alignment-kt-layoutparams).
- [`snapAndTidyLocal`](visualization.md#alignment-kt--snapandtidylocal) snaps near-equal sizes and edges together, snaps positions, then pushes
  overlapping rectangles apart.
- [`routeAndTidyLocal`](visualization.md#alignment-kt--routeandtidylocal) also takes the connections between rectangles as [`EdgeId`](visualization.md#alignment-kt-edgeid)s. It snaps
  sizes and edges, arranges the rectangles in layers along those edges ([`RouteParams`](visualization.md#alignment-kt-routeparams)), then
  runs the tidy pass and an optional final columnizing pass.

[`snapAndTidyLocal`](visualization.md#alignment-kt--snapandtidylocal) and [`routeAndTidyLocal`](visualization.md#alignment-kt--routeandtidylocal) can translate their result back so the group's
centroid ([`CentroidMode`](visualization.md#alignment-kt-centroidmode)) does not move: `preserve` for the first, `preserveCentroid` in
[`RouteParams`](visualization.md#alignment-kt-routeparams) for the second. [`installAlignment`](visualization.md#alignment-kt--installalignment) runs on each new root and adds the `align`,
`snap_tidy` and `route` actions, which call these with fixed parameters and write the results
to the selected boxes' `frame`s; `align` also restores the centroid.

## DarkThemeColour.kt { #darkthemecolour-kt }

Colour correction for marks written from code, so that they show as asked under the drawing layer's dark
theme rather than as their inverted, hue-rotated selves.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/notation/DarkThemeColour.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/notation/DarkThemeColour/)

### DarkThemeColour { #darkthemecolour-kt-darkthemecolour }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">DarkThemeColour</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/notation/DarkThemeColour/#L22)

Colours as the drawing layer shows them. Excalidraw's dark theme draws the scene through the CSS filter `invert(93%) hue-rotate(180deg)` (`theme="dark"` in `tools/excalidraw-bundle/entry.jsx`), so a colour stored on an element is not the colour on screen. Per channel the inversion is `0.93 - 0.86 c`; the hue rotation is the CSS filter matrix `H` for 180°.

## Notation.kt { #notation-kt }

The box-facing API for the drawing layer: [`notation`](visualization.md#notation-kt--notation) reads the document's Excalidraw scene as [`Mark`](visualization.md#notation-kt-mark)s,
writes marks owned by the box through a `notation { }` block ([`NotationBuilder`](visualization.md#notation-kt-notationbuilder)), changes existing ones
with [`Notation.edit`](visualization.md#notation-kt--notation--edit), and runs callbacks when a person draws.

Marks a box writes are replaced when that box re-runs, so a re-run redraws rather than accumulates.
Reactions such as `notation.onStroke { }` fire only for changes made by hand in a client, not for marks
written from code. Coverage is in `NotationTest` and `NotationIntersectionTest`; the full API is in
`dev_docs/NOTATION.md`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/notation/Notation.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/notation/Notation/)

**Used in:** [Drawn Strokes Become Paint](../chain_drawn_paint.md), [Drawing and Notation](../drawing_and_notation.md), [A Drawn Score, Heard](../chain_drawn_score.md)

## NotationGeometry.kt { #notationgeometry-kt }

Cutting the drawing with a line: the geometry behind reading notation by intersection — a
vertical line is an instant, a horizontal one a pitch (or whatever a [`NotationSpace`](visualization.md#notationgeometry-kt-notationspace) says the
axes mean).

Every mark is flattened once per scene revision into world-space polylines with its rotation
applied (`MarkGeometry`); probes then only walk segments. The results are plain values, safe to
keep and to read from any thread.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/notation/NotationGeometry.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/notation/NotationGeometry/)

### NotationSpace { #notationgeometry-kt-notationspace }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">NotationSpace</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">notation</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Notation</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">region</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Rect</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ClosedFloatingPointRange</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ClosedFloatingPointRange</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">defining</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">{</span> <span class="kc">null</span> <span class="p">}</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/notation/NotationGeometry/#L212)

A region of the drawing with its own axes — a score, a graph, a map. Horizontal position in the region becomes the [`x`](visualization.md#notationgeometry-kt--notationspace--x) range and vertical position the [`y`](visualization.md#notationgeometry-kt--notationspace--y) range, so `notation.space("score", x = 0.0..8.0, y = 84.0..48.0)` reads the frame named "score" as eight beats across and a MIDI pitch range down (high at the top, because Field's y grows downward).

## NotationScene.kt { #notationscene-kt }

The drawing layer's scene as immutable data: [`NotationScene`](visualization.md#notationscene-kt-notationscene) parses and re-serializes the root box's
`drawing` property, [`NotationChange`](visualization.md#notationscene-kt-notationchange) describes what differs between two scenes, and [`MarkType`](visualization.md#notationscene-kt-marktype) names the
Excalidraw element kinds.

Merging two copies of a scene keeps, for each element id, the copy Excalidraw's own version rule prefers,
so the server can reconcile a client's drawing with marks written from code.

## NotationServer.kt { #notationserver-kt }

The server end of the drawing layer: [`installNotationHandlers`](visualization.md#notationserver-kt--installnotationhandlers) registers the websocket handlers that
receive each client's scene and selection, merge the scene into the document's copy, and pass what a
person changed on to the box reactions and to arrow anchoring.

Anchoring ties a mark, or each end of an arrow, to the box under it, so the drawing follows when boxes
move. The drawing layer's **Anchor Drawing to Boxes** command applies it to the selection.

## StrokeLayerFrames.kt { #strokelayerframes-kt }

What a window is sent to draw the stroke layer: every living stroke's lines as compact JSON, and
the point index the strokes use to find each other.

[`StrokeSketch`](visualization.md#strokesketch-kt-strokesketch) calls both. [`StrokeLayerFrames.indexedPositions`](visualization.md#strokelayerframes-kt--strokelayerframes--indexedpositions) runs once per stroke per physics
step, over the lines that stroke has just drawn, and the flat x, y array it returns is what
[`Stroke.closestOutput`](visualization.md#strokesketch-kt--stroke--closestoutput) searches on the step after. [`StrokeLayerFrames.encode`](visualization.md#strokelayerframes-kt--strokelayerframes--encode) runs once per
published frame, and its JSON reaches every window showing the document as `stroke-layer-frame`;
`strokeLayer.kt` in the frontend draws it.

Only what a canvas needs crosses the wire. Coordinates are world units rounded to a tenth, colours
arrive as CSS rather than as vectors, and a per-node colour or dot radius is sent only when some
node sets one. Overshoot ticks ([`FLine.overshoot`](visualization.md#strokeverbs-kt--overshoot)) are worked out here and sent as finished
segments. `StrokeVerbsTest` asserts the paths, colours, dots and ticks of a frame, and that an
ignored line stays out of the index.

## StrokeSketch.kt { #strokesketch-kt }

Living strokes: each stroke drawn by hand on the drawing layer becomes an animated, sounding object
running code of its own, after the madp line demo.

A box takes the pen with [`eachStroke`](visualization.md#strokesketch-kt--eachstroke). Each stroke then drawn with the drawing layer's pencil is
taken off the scene and becomes a [`Stroke`](visualization.md#strokesketch-kt-stroke): physics points that start where the hand went, the
block of the box that held the pen when it was drawn (later edits do not reach it), a `draw { t -> }`
called sixty times a second, and an optional pattern playing through dough. What the strokes draw
is shown on the **stroke layer**, a canvas in world coordinates between Field's background and its
boxes, which fades towards transparent for trails.

One [`StrokeSketch`](visualization.md#strokesketch-kt-strokesketch) per document keeps the strokes, the pen and the clock. Its frames go to each
window showing the document as `stroke-layer-frame`, one at a time: the next is sent once the window
answers `stroke-layer-ack`, so a slow window is never flooded.

## StrokeVerbs.kt { #strokeverbs-kt }

The drawing vocabulary of a living stroke: Perlin noise, curve maths, and the verbs that turn a
list of points into an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline).

[`StrokeVerbs`](visualization.md#strokeverbs-kt-strokeverbs) carries the verbs, and [`Stroke`](visualization.md#strokesketch-kt-stroke) inherits it, so `eachStroke { }` code calls them
directly. Some are short names over the shared geometry: `smooth` is [`catmullRomCentripetal`](graphics.md#flinegeometry-kt--catmullromcentripetal) and
`atomize` is [`FLine.byAtomizing`](graphics.md#flinegeometry-kt--byatomizing), while `wiggle` and `transformTo` have a curve form of their own
and a line form that calls [`FLine.byWiggling`](graphics.md#flinegeometry-kt--bywiggling) and [`FLine.byTransformingTo`](graphics.md#flinegeometry-kt--bytransformingto). The noise, the
resampling and the rest of the curve arithmetic are this file's own.

The three [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) properties here are read by the stroke layer rather than by any verb.
[`FLine.overshoot`](visualization.md#strokeverbs-kt--overshoot) runs each open subpath of a line past its ends, a node's `overshoot` overrides
that for the subpath it ends, and [`FLine.ignore`](visualization.md#strokeverbs-kt--ignore) keeps a line out of the point index
[`Stroke.closestOutput`](visualization.md#strokesketch-kt--stroke--closestoutput) searches, so a guide or a stitch does not attract the strokes around it.

`StrokeVerbsTest` pins the resampling, the curve maths and the noise.

## CharGrid.kt { #chargrid-kt }

A grid of glyphs that box code writes into, cell by cell, shown in an output panel: generative
text art in the spirit of 10 PRINT, ported from the madp charGrid demo.

The program writes **glyph indices** with `SET`, and a charset string (`glyphs`) turns each index
into a character; a cell can also carry a CSS colour and raw CSS such as `transform:rotate(45deg)`.
[`charGrid`](visualization.md#chargrid-kt--chargrid) runs its block once per tick with the previous tick readable through `PREV`; [`charStream`](visualization.md#chargrid-kt--charstream)
runs one long suspending program in which every `SET` waits for the next tick. A glyph can be a
dough sound ([`Box.sound`](synthesis.md#doughlive-kt--sound)), so every `SET` of it plays. The panel pulls only the cells that changed
since it last asked ([`CharGridBuffer.update`](visualization.md#chargrid-kt--chargridbuffer--update)), so a 200 × 100 grid at 24 fps sends a frame's
changes, not the whole grid.

## LiveOutputIframe.kt { #liveoutputiframe-kt }

Script access to the iframe inside a box's output area as the Electron tab shows it:
[`outputIframe`](visualization.md#liveoutputiframe-kt--outputiframe) resolves a box and channel to a [`LiveOutputIframe`](visualization.md#liveoutputiframe-kt-liveoutputiframe), whose calls (JavaScript
evaluation, raw CDP, navigation) return futures so the runloop is not blocked while the tab answers.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/output/LiveOutputIframe.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/output/LiveOutputIframe/)

## MarkdownOutput.kt { #markdownoutput-kt }

Markdown output for box output areas: [`markdown`](visualization.md#markdownoutput-kt--markdown) renders GitHub-flavoured markdown, with raw HTML,
side-by-side `:::row` columns and `{role:text}` spans, into a styled card using Field's design
tokens. [`FieldMarkdown`](visualization.md#markdownoutput-kt-fieldmarkdown) holds the renderer and its full syntax; [`md`](visualization.md#markdownoutput-kt--md) and [`mdEscape`](visualization.md#markdownoutput-kt--mdescape) escape a value
for interpolation.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/output/MarkdownOutput.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/output/MarkdownOutput/)

**Used in:** [Visualizers, Displays, and Little Instruments](../visualizers.md), [Measuring dependence between two signals](../statistics_examples.md)

## callbacks.kt { #callbacks-kt }

Per-box callback tables that run when a box's frame, viewport, name or children change.

Box code adds a named entry to `onFrameChange`, `onViewportChange`, `onNameChange` or `onTopologyChange`. A frame or name callback receives the current and incoming value and returns the value to keep. A callback that throws is reported as an error on the box, and the remaining callbacks for that change are skipped.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/output/callbacks.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/output/callbacks/)

## decorations.kt { #decorations-kt }

Editor decorations driven from running code: [`RawDecoration`](visualization.md#decorations-kt-rawdecoration) marks a span of a box's source in
Monaco, and the `Marker` extensions here — [`histogram`](visualization.md#decorations-kt--histogram), [`history`](visualization.md#decorations-kt--history), [`stats`](visualization.md#decorations-kt--stats), [`liveNumber`](visualization.md#decorations-kt--livenumber), [`toggle`](visualization.md#decorations-kt--toggle),
[`beep`](visualization.md#decorations-kt--beep), [`bop`](visualization.md#decorations-kt--bop) — attach live values and clickable widgets to the line that called them.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/output/decorations.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/output/decorations/)

## outputs.kt { #outputs-kt }

Output areas and controls for box code: [`HasOutput`](visualization.md#outputs-kt-hasoutput) and the `display` channels, progress bars and
[`withProgress`](visualization.md#outputs-kt--withprogress), [`streamProcess`](visualization.md#outputs-kt--streamprocess) for running external commands into a panel, the `tree`, `column`
and `logs` embeds, and the controls DSL — [`slider`](visualization.md#outputs-kt--slider), [`checkbox`](visualization.md#outputs-kt--checkbox), [`stringInput`](visualization.md#outputs-kt--stringinput), [`colorPicker`](visualization.md#outputs-kt--colorpicker),
[`button`](visualization.md#outputs-kt--button), [`controlGroup`](visualization.md#outputs-kt--controlgroup) and [`syncToProperty`](visualization.md#outputs-kt--synctoproperty).

Each control renders into a named output channel (`controls` by default) and calls back into the
box when the browser reports a change.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/output/outputs.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/output/outputs/)

**Used in:** [Visualizers, Displays, and Little Instruments](../visualizers.md), [The keyframe editor: drawing a value over time](../keyframe_editor.md), [Box Output: print, display and channels](../box_output.md)

Like every method here, it is a no-op outside a box, while disabled, or during the grace period. |

Idempotent, and a no-op when inert or already completed — so an outer `finally` won't cut short the linger of a bar that finished on its own. This is the abort path: a bar that never reached 100% is removed at once. Sends nothing if the bar was never shown (i.e. it lived and died entirely inside the grace period). |

## terminalOutput.kt { #terminaloutput-kt }

A real terminal in a box's output area: [`terminal`](visualization.md#terminaloutput-kt--terminal) starts a process in a panel and returns a
[`FieldTerminal`](visualization.md#terminaloutput-kt-fieldterminal) that box code can type into, read, and kill. The process outlives its panel, which
re-attaches with its scrollback.

## AudienceBuilder.kt { #audiencebuilder-kt }

The HTML an audience slide is written in: kotlinx.html's builders, with scoped Markdown,
stylesheets and two picture layouts added.

[`SlideStepBuilder.audience`](visualization.md#presentation-kt--audience) runs its block against an [`AudienceBuilder`](visualization.md#audiencebuilder-kt-audiencebuilder), which is a kotlinx.html
`DIV` carrying the slide's class, so every standard tag works inside it, along with Kotlin's own
loops, functions and completion. Text added with `+` is escaped by the library; `"# Heading".md`
renders Markdown instead, and the unary plus on the [`AudienceMarkdown`](visualization.md#audiencebuilder-kt-audiencemarkdown) it returns inserts the
generated tags unescaped. That pair is how one slide mixes written prose with built HTML.

Use [`AudienceBuilder.div`](visualization.md#audiencebuilder-kt--audiencebuilder--div) rather than kotlinx.html's own `div` for a nested container, since only
this one keeps the Markdown syntax available inside it. [`AudienceBuilder.stylesheet`](visualization.md#audiencebuilder-kt--audiencebuilder--stylesheet) links a CSS
file from the document's files directory; the audience fetches it past the browser cache each time
a slide is drawn, so an edit to it appears on Refresh slide.
[`AudienceBuilder.fullScreenImage`](visualization.md#audiencebuilder-kt--audiencebuilder--fullscreenimage) and [`AudienceBuilder.imageBeside`](visualization.md#audiencebuilder-kt--audiencebuilder--imagebeside) are the picture layouts. Both
want alt text and take an optional visible credit, and [`AudienceImageFit`](visualization.md#audiencebuilder-kt-audienceimagefit) chooses between
containing the whole picture and cropping it to fill.

## Presentation.kt { #presentation-kt }

Giving a talk from a Field document: [`Box.presentation`](visualization.md#presentation-kt--presentation) builds the same steps a `slideShow` does,
and each step can carry a slide for a separate audience display.

A step's audience surface is HTML, a real webpage, a YouTube embed, or another document in the
workspace. Write the HTML with [`SlideStepBuilder.audience`](visualization.md#presentation-kt--audience) for kotlinx.html's type-safe builders
(see [`AudienceBuilder`](visualization.md#audiencebuilder-kt-audiencebuilder)), with [`SlideStepBuilder.audienceHtml`](visualization.md#presentation-kt--audiencehtml) for a fragment you already have, or
with [`SlideStepBuilder.audienceMarkdown`](visualization.md#presentation-kt--audiencemarkdown). [`SlideStepBuilder.audienceWebpage`](visualization.md#presentation-kt--audiencewebpage) and
[`SlideStepBuilder.audienceYouTube`](visualization.md#presentation-kt--audienceyoutube) put a page or a video in an isolated native Electron view, and
[`SlideStepBuilder.audienceDocument`](visualization.md#presentation-kt--audiencedocument) opens another workspace document with its own editor, outputs
and guide. A step with no audience surface shows its note HTML, templates and all, so a guide
written for a reader presents without being rewritten.

[`SlideShowInstance.present`](visualization.md#presentation-kt--present) starts the talk. Each step publishes a `presentation-state` message to
the windows showing the host box's document, and Field's Electron app opens the audience and
presenter windows from it; in a browser the document and its guides still work, but there is no
separate display. Running the host box again rebuilds the talk and keeps the current step where it
can. Anything bound for Electron is checked before it gets there: a webpage needs an HTTP or HTTPS
URL with a host, a document a plain name in the current workspace, a video the eleven-character
YouTube id, and a fractional rect has to sit inside the audience window.

[Presenting with Field](../presentation_studio.md) is the guide to writing one.

## SlideShow.kt { #slideshow-kt }

SlideShow - A DSL for creating guided tours through Field documents

This system supports creating interactive guides with:
- Step-by-step navigation
- Custom link callbacks that execute Kotlin code
- Template system for displaying live data
- Annotations and visual highlighting

Example usage:
```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
// Set up properties that templates can reference
var counter = 0
this.properties["counter"] = counter

slideShow {
    step("Introduction") {
        note("""
            <h2>Welcome!</h2>
            <p>Counter value: {{counter}}</p>
            <p><a href="#custom:increment">Click to increment</a></p>
            <p><a href="#slideshow:next">Continue →</a></p>
        """)

        // Register a callback for the custom link
        linkCallback("increment") {
            counter++
            here.properties["counter"] = counter
            // Refresh to show new value
            show.goToStep(show.currentStepIndex)
        }

        selectBox(myBox)
    }
}
```

**Custom Links:**
Use `#custom:callbackName` in href attributes, then register with `linkCallback("callbackName") { ... }`

**Templates:**
Use `{{propertyName}}` to reference box properties or Kotlin variables in the guide's scope

**Navigation Links:**
- `#slideshow:next` - Go to next step
- `#slideshow:previous` - Go to previous step
- `#slideshow:home` - Go to first step
- `#slideshow:stop` - Stop the slideshow

## AudioVisualizer.kt { #audiovisualizer-kt }

The recorded-audio waveform player: a zoomable, seekable view of a recording, as one
self-contained HTML fragment for a box output.

It shows audio that already exists, rather than a spectrum or a live meter, with the interaction
an editor expects (wheel to zoom, drag to pan, click to seek, a playhead that tracks playback)
and the browser's own transport underneath.

What it draws is a min/max envelope of the *visible* window, not the whole file decimated. Where
a server can summarise a window ([`AudioVisualizerSource.waveformUrl`](visualization.md#audiovisualizer-kt--audiovisualizersource--waveformurl) — Field Audio's waveform
endpoint, for instance) the component asks for one envelope per view, so an hour-long recording
costs the same as a bar of it; where there is no server it decodes the clip in the browser and
does the same arithmetic locally. Min/max rather than an average is what keeps a single-sample
click visible in a window drawn at 1000 points.

Start from `Box.displayAudio` for a URL, `Box.displayAudioSamples` for a `FloatArray` you
generated, or `Box.displayAudioBytes` for an encoded clip you have in memory.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/AudioVisualizer.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/visualization/AudioVisualizer/)

**Used in:** [Visualizers, Displays, and Little Instruments](../visualizers.md), [Multi-instrument transcription with MuScriptor](../audio_ai_muscriptor.md), [Render Field music, then analyse it](../audio_render_analysis.md)

## DataFrameCharts.kt { #dataframecharts-kt }

A typed frame, charting its own columns.

`DataFrameVisualizer` already teaches a frame to render as a [`Table`](visualization.md#tables-kt-table) for `.h` and to stream its
rows for `.h2`, which is the right compact form: a frame is rows and columns first. What it had no
answer for is the other question a reader has about a numeric column, which is *what shape is it*.

This is that answer, and it is thin — nine lines of column selection over [`Chart`](visualization.md#charts-kt-chart).
The interesting decision is which columns, and the rule is the one that makes `frame.chart()` with
no arguments do the obvious thing:

 - a **numeric** x column and the rest numeric: lines against it, one series per column;
 - a **categorical** first column (strings, or anything not numeric) and one numeric column: bars,
   with the category names on the axis — which is what a `groupBy(...).count()` looks like, and the
   commonest frame anyone actually plots;
 - no x column named and none obvious: the row index.

Non-numeric cells inside a numeric column become gaps rather than zeroes. A missing measurement is
not a measurement of zero, and drawing it as one is the single most common way a plot lies.

## DataFrameVisualizer.kt { #dataframevisualizer-kt }

Makes Kotlin DataFrame values render as Field values (`.h`, `.h2`, `display` and box return
values) without DataFrame having to know Field exists.

`DataFrame` is a third-party interface, so it cannot implement [`ToHTML`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-tohtml) the way [`Table`](visualization.md#tables-kt-table) and [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img)
do. Both registries exist for exactly this: [`ValuePrinterRegistry`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-valueprinterregistry) for the compact `.h` form, and
[`H2ValueRegistry`](visualization.md#lazyvaluevisualizer-kt-h2valueregistry) for `.h2`. Everything here is a thin adapter onto primitives that already exist,
so a frame gets the same styling, the same expander and the same paging as every other value.

### The compact `.h` form

[`table`](visualization.md#tables-kt--table) already renders a column-oriented table in Field's output style, so a frame's compact
form is that table over the first `HEAD_ROWS` rows, plus a line giving the shape. Only the head is
touched: each column is indexed for its first `HEAD_ROWS` cells rather than the frame being
materialised, so printing a million-row frame costs about what printing ten rows costs.

### The `.h2` scroller

[`H2ValueSnapshot`](visualization.md#lazyvaluevisualizer-kt-h2valuesnapshot) adapts one value into another for the lazy renderer rather than producing HTML.
So `.h2` on a frame adapts it into a private list-of-rows view that reads a row only when asked,
and the h2 explorer (`h2explorer.kt`, reached as an iframe onto `/h2-explorer?root=<token>` and fed
over the `/ws` `__h2_explorer__` channel) streams windows of it by index. The server holds the
frame rather than a rendering of it behind an `.h2` token, and each scroll materialises only the
window being looked at, which is what makes a large frame a scroller instead of a large HTML dump.
`ValueVisualizer`'s `/lazy-value-fragment` renderer is a separate path, for expanding a value in
place rather than scrolling one.

Going through the registries rather than a bespoke widget also means a frame nested inside another
value, a list of frames or a data class with a frame field, expands with the same machinery.

### Where the adapters get registered

`install` is idempotent and runs during server start-up. A bare `jvm-main` harness does not run
that, so tests call it explicitly; `DataFrameVisualizerSmokeTest` is the worked example.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/DataFrameVisualizer.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/visualization/DataFrameVisualizer/)

## DataFrameVisualizerSmokeTest.kt { #dataframevisualizersmoketest-kt }

Checks that DataFrame values render through Field's value registries — [`DataFrameVisualizer`](visualization.md#dataframevisualizer-kt-dataframevisualizer).

The assertions are deliberately about *dispatch and laziness* rather than exact markup, which
would make this a change-detector on the table renderer:

 - the registry is reached at all (a frame must not fall through to `toString()`);
 - `.h` shows a head and says how much it is hiding, without materialising the frame;
 - `.h` on a large frame produces BOUNDED output — it must not contain the last row's data. That
   is the observable form of "only the head was rendered". An earlier version of this test counted
   lambda invocations on an added column instead and passed with a count of zero, because `add`
   materialises its column eagerly and cell access never re-invokes the lambda: the assertion was
   vacuous. Output content is the property worth pinning, since it is what a box actually shows.

`install()` is called explicitly because `Server.main` — which calls it in the app — does not run
in a bare jvm-main harness.

## H2DomainAdapters.kt { #h2domainadapters-kt }

`.h2` adapters for the Field types where the *reflective* default in `H2Reflect.kt` reads badly.

`H2Reflect` lifted `.h2` from "types someone registered" to "everything", and for a data class or
a plain domain object a property tree is exactly right. Four families it is wrong for, each for
its own reason:

 - **[`Box`](workspace.md#boxes-kt-box)** — reflection would touch `Box.ki`, a `lazyVar` that *builds a K2 REPL engine on
   read*. Exploring a box would compile one. This is the concrete case behind the side-effect
   limit `H2Reflect`'s KDoc admits it cannot detect, and the reason `Box` is served here.
 - **[`Functions.Fn`](math.md#functions-kt--functions--fn)** — its only non-derived field is a private `(Double) -> Double`. A function's
   content is its *values*, so the adapter samples it.
 - **[`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline)** — a polyline's content is its node list, and `nodes` is one property among four.
 - **`Throwable`** — a `java.*` type, refused by the platform-package narrowing, and the value a
   box produces most often when something is wrong.

Each adapter returns a shape the existing explorer machinery already renders well —
a `LinkedHashMap` gets map paging, and a `List<Map<String, Any?>>` hits the explorer's RECORD
mode and becomes a real table with one column per key. That is deliberate: an adapter that
invented its own rendering would have to be maintained in three places.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/H2DomainAdapters.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/visualization/H2DomainAdapters/)
