## H2Reflect.kt { #h2reflect-kt }

The reflective half of `.h2`: what a domain object's *children* are, computed once and shared by
every surface that shows them.

`.h2` renders a value three separate times — the `Browsable` tree behind `/tree` and `/browse`,
the row/column stream behind the embedded `/h2-explorer` iframe, and the summary line in the
widget itself. This file computes the children all three read, reflectively and for any type. A
per-type [`H2ValueSnapshot`](visualization.md#lazyvaluevisualizer-kt-h2valuesnapshot) adapter is the alternative, and stays the route for a type whose
getters this cannot walk safely; without either, a non-collection falls through
[`LazyValueVisualizer.visualize`](visualization.md#lazyvaluevisualizer-kt--lazyvaluevisualizer--visualize)'s opening guard to `ValueVisualizer` and `.h2` renders as `.h`.

`properties` is the *single* enumerator, so `/tree` and the iframe cannot disagree about how many
fields a value has.

### Getters are opaque

A `KProperty1` getter is opaque: there is no way to tell a field read from a computed property
that opens a file, allocates a GPU buffer or builds a K2 REPL engine. `Box.ki` is a `lazyVar`
that compiles on read, which is why [`Box`](workspace.md#boxes-kt-box) is served by a hand-written adapter in
`H2DomainAdapters.kt` rather than by this file. The two narrowings in `readsWellInline` (platform
packages, and types whose `.h` rendering *is* the value) mitigate the general case rather than
settling it. If a type's getters are expensive or effectful, give it an adapter.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/H2Reflect.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/visualization/H2Reflect/)

## ImagingVisualizer.kt { #imagingvisualizer-kt }

Inline visualizers for the CPU imaging and computer-vision family (`afield.stdlib/imaging*.kt`):
what a gradient, a pyramid, a flow field or a list of corners looks like when a box evaluates one.

The imaging layer is around 250 public symbols of raster and feature code, and [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img) is the only
one of its types that carries a picture of its own. Everything else falls through to a reflective
object tree unless something here claims it, and there a list of forty [`Corner`](imaging.md#imaging-features-kt-corner)s is a wall of
`{x=…, y=…, response=…}` and a [`GaussianPyramid`](imaging.md#imaging-filters-kt-gaussianpyramid) is `GaussianPyramid@3f1a2b`. Those are exactly
the values you want to look at.

### Where this hooks in

Three one-line hooks, small enough that this file can grow without touching `ValueVisualizer.kt`:

 - `Img.toHTML` delegates to [`img`](visualization.md#imagingvisualizer-kt--imagingvisualizer--img). [`Img`](imaging.md#imaging-kt-img) implements [`ToHTML`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-tohtml), which `ValueVisualizer` dispatches
   before its built-in table, so improving the `Img` picture has to happen there.
 - `ValueVisualizer.visualizeBuiltIn`'s fallback branch tries [`format`](visualization.md#imagingvisualizer-kt--imagingvisualizer--format) first, which covers the
   non-data classes ([`Gradient`](imaging.md#imaging-filters-kt-gradient), [`GaussianPyramid`](imaging.md#imaging-filters-kt-gaussianpyramid), [`LaplacianPyramid`](imaging.md#imaging-filters-kt-laplacianpyramid), [`FlowField`](imaging.md#imaging-geometry-kt-flowfield),
   [`ComponentLabelling`](imaging.md#imaging-features-kt-componentlabelling)).
 - `ValueVisualizer.formatList` tries [`formatList`](visualization.md#imagingvisualizer-kt--imagingvisualizer--formatlist) first, which covers the homogeneous detector
   outputs (`List<Corner>`, `List<HoughLine>`, `List<HoughCircle>`, `List<FlowVector>`,
   `List<Img>`).

### Turning a float image into pixels

The family is float-channel and unbounded: a Sobel `dx`, a Laplacian and a
difference-of-Gaussians are legitimately signed, an unnormalised response legitimately exceeds 1,
and a division somewhere upstream legitimately produces a NaN. A visualizer that clamps all of
those to `0..1` shows a flat white or a flat black rectangle and tells you nothing, so the raster
renderer picks one of three modes:

 - **direct** — every finite sample already sits in `0..1`. Shown as-is; nothing is rescaled.
 - **signed ±m** — some finite sample is negative. The range is made symmetric about zero
   (`m = max(|min|, |max|)`) so that zero is a fixed, recognisable colour. A 1-channel image is
   additionally run through the `coolwarm` diverging ramp from [`Colormaps`](graphics.md#colormaps-kt-colormaps) (blue negative, pale
   zero, red positive), because grey cannot carry the sign of a gradient. Multi-channel signed
   data is offset and scaled per sample without a ramp.
 - **auto-ranged** — everything is non-negative but the maximum exceeds 1. Linearly rescaled, with
   the data's true range printed beside it, so a bright pixel is never mistaken for 1.0.

The caption names the mode whenever the mode rescaled something; the statistics table inside the
disclosure names it in every case, including the fourth one, where no sample is finite at all.

Non-finite samples (NaN, ±∞) are counted, excluded from every statistic, and painted **magenta**
so they are impossible to miss. Excluding them is what keeps one NaN out of the minimum and the
maximum, where it would take the whole display range with it and quantise to a uniformly black
thumbnail captioned `range NaN…NaN`.

A 4-channel image is drawn over a **checkerboard**, so transparent and black are distinguishable.

### The disclosure

Each raster visualizer carries a closed `<details>` with the per-channel strip, a per-channel
histogram computed over the full-resolution samples, and the numeric stats. It is a plain
`<details>` element rather than a `lazy-value-fragment` expander link, so it needs no running
server and works identically in a live box, in a docs capture and in a saved HTML file.

## LazyValueVisualizer.kt { #lazyvaluevisualizer-kt }

The lazy half of value display: rather than inline a large structure, show one summary line plus
links into the server-side browsers.

[`LazyValueVisualizer.visualize`](visualization.md#lazyvaluevisualizer-kt--lazyvaluevisualizer--visualize) — reached in a box as [`h2`](visualization.md#lazyvaluevisualizer-kt--h2) — passes anything small or
unrecognised straight to `ValueVisualizer`. For maps, lists, arrays and `FloatBuffer` /
`IntBuffer` it instead retains the value under a token and emits a summary, `outliner` and
`columns` links, and an embedded `/h2-explorer` iframe. Those tokens live in an in-memory
retention table (10 minutes, 256 entries), so the links only resolve against the running server
and go stale after that.

The private `Browsable` wrappers behind those routes page rather than copy: children are grouped
into range-labelled directories of at most 96 entries, and a map with more than 20,000 entries is
iterated on demand instead of snapshotted. [`registerH2Value`](visualization.md#lazyvaluevisualizer-kt--registerh2value) adds a per-type adapter returning an
[`H2ValueSnapshot`](visualization.md#lazyvaluevisualizer-kt-h2valuesnapshot) when a type should be summarised or unwrapped differently, and
`lazyInlineExpanderHtml` is the inline "… +N more" link `ValueVisualizer` emits for elided
content.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/LazyValueVisualizer.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/visualization/LazyValueVisualizer/)

## SignalViewer.kt { #signalviewer-kt }

A zoomable viewer for functions of time: each [`SignalChannel`](visualization.md#signalviewer-kt-signalchannel) is a lane drawn as a min/max
envelope, resampled as you zoom.

[`SignalViewer`](visualization.md#signalviewer-kt-signalviewer) holds the lanes and answers the browser's window queries; [`Box.displaySignal`](visualization.md#signalviewer-kt--displaysignal)
shows it in an output channel and keeps it alive while it is visible. A lane built with
[`certifiedSignalChannel`](visualization.md#signalviewer-kt--certifiedsignalchannel) also draws the interval-arithmetic bound of its function behind the
sampled envelope.

A range-query source for the frontend signal viewer. Like AudioVisualizer, it sends only the visible envelope; unlike recorded audio, functions are evaluated more finely as you zoom in. Envelopes preserve extrema on the sampling grid, not arbitrarily narrow features between samples. Keep this object alive while its HTML is visible, or use Box.displaySignal, which does so for you.

## ValueVisualizer.kt { #valuevisualizer-kt }

The default value display for Field output areas: a Kotlin value in, a compact HTML fragment out.

[`ValueVisualizer.visualize`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt--valuevisualizer--visualize) is the entry point; [`Any.h`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt--h) and [`Box.viz`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt--viz) are how it is usually
reached — `.h` hands back the fragment, `viz` displays it into a channel of a live box. A type
can take over its own rendering either by implementing [`ToHTML`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-tohtml) or by registering a printer with
[`registerValuePrinter`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt--registervalueprinter); both are trusted to return well-formed HTML, while ordinary strings,
characters, keys and reflected values are escaped here.

Output is bounded — [`ValueVisualizer`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-valuevisualizer)'s own KDoc below covers dispatch order, the
built-in formatters and the size limits. Whatever those limits elide (the tail of a long string
or list, extra fields of an object) becomes an expander link, resolved later by
`renderLazyFragment` from the server's `/lazy-value-fragment` route, so the rest of the value is
only ever rendered if someone asks for it.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/ValueVisualizer.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/visualization/ValueVisualizer/)

**Used in:** [Visualizers, Displays, and Little Instruments](../visualizers.md), [Agent transcript gallery](../agent_transcripts.md), [DataFrames in a Box](../dataframe.md)

## charts.kt { #charts-kt }

Plots — the structure, the scales, and the one renderer for them.

[`Chart`](visualization.md#charts-kt-chart) is to a plot what [`Table`](visualization.md#tables-kt-table) is to a grid: build it, and it arrives on screen in the repo's
style with no markup in the way. It implements [`ToHTML`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-tohtml), so `display(channel, chart)`, `chart.h`
and a box whose last expression is a `Chart` all render through [`Chart.toHTML`](visualization.md#charts-kt--chart--tohtml); [`Box.showChart`](visualization.md#charts-kt--showchart)
is the terse form.

### This file or `plotly.kt`

`plotly.kt` — `showSignals`, `linePlot`, `scatter`, `violin` — is the default, and better at being
a chart: real text rather than glyph geometry, a plot that reflows to its panel instead of being
fitted and centred, and log, subplot and box axes this file does not carry. Reach for a [`Chart`](visualization.md#charts-kt-chart)
for the three things Plotly cannot do: composing a plot with other FLine geometry in one drawing
under a shared transform, picking, and [`Chart.expect`](visualization.md#charts-kt--chart--expect).

Axis labels here are real glyph geometry (`labelLines`), filled and with their counters intact,
because `showPlaneGrid` has nowhere to put text. [`niceTicks`](visualization.md#charts-kt--niceticks) is Heckbert's nice-number tick
algorithm in public. `dev_docs/chart_primitive.md` holds the Plotly comparison capture and the
survey of what each medium in the repo was drawing for itself.

### Marks pick themselves up

`Box.lines` switches to the interactive SVG renderer the moment any line carries
[`FLine.onClick`](graphics.md#standarddrawing-kt--onclick) or [`FLine.hoverColor`](graphics.md#standarddrawing-kt--hovercolor) (`someSkiko.kt`). Point and bar marks set both, so hovering
a bar and clicking a datum need no configuration — see [`Chart.pickable`](visualization.md#charts-kt--chart--pickable) for the escape hatch and
the cost.

### Chart.expect

Exactly as in [`Table`](visualization.md#tables-kt-table). A plot in a doc or a live box usually carries a claim — "no residual
exceeds 1e-6", "every voice stayed inside the guard band". State the claim and it is *drawn* as a
band, the data outside it recolours, the footnote says how many points broke it, and
[`Chart.deviations`](visualization.md#charts-kt--chart--deviations) hands the same list to a test.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/charts.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/visualization/charts/)

## heatmap.kt { #heatmap-kt }

A rectangular array of numbers as a colour-mapped picture in a box output, in one call.

The file is two layers. [`heatmapImage`](visualization.md#heatmap-kt--heatmapimage) is pure: a rectangular matrix in, a [`RasterImage`](visualization.md#heatmap-kt-rasterimage) of ARGB
pixels out, with the colour scale, the optional log transform, the bilinear upsample and the
overlay trace all resolved there, so a test or a docs capture can render one without a Box.
`Box.showHeatmap` adds the two steps a box wants, encoding to PNG and displaying it into an
output channel, and returns the bytes so the caller can save or re-display them. `Box.showImage`
is that same second layer over a pixel buffer you already have.

Two conventions decide which way up the picture comes out. The matrix is read row-major, outer
index the row and inner index the column, so rows are the vertical axis; and `flipY` defaults to
true, drawing row 0 at the bottom, which is what a spectrogram's frequency bins want. A
spectrogram stored the other way round, frame-outer and bin-inner, is the `transpose = true`
case: frames become x and bins become y.

Colour is a [`Colormaps`](graphics.md#colormaps-kt-colormaps) name and a range. Under `normalize` the range is the data's own minimum
and maximum; `vmin` and `vmax` pin it instead, which is what makes two captures comparable;
`logScale` runs each value through `log10(max(v, 1e-12))` first, for magnitude spectra and
anything else spanning orders of magnitude.

## plotly.kt { #plotly-kt }

Plotly helpers — the short way to get a chart out of a box, wrapping `space.kscience.plotly`.

`linePlot`, [`scatter`](visualization.md#plotly-kt--scatter), [`scatterSized`](visualization.md#plotly-kt--scattersized) and [`violin`](visualization.md#plotly-kt--violin) cover the common shapes (lists of numbers,
`Vec2`, `Vec3`) and hand back a `Plot` already run through [`darkMode`](visualization.md#plotly-kt--darkmode), the repo dark theme with
data-first margins. [`showSignals`](visualization.md#plotly-kt--showsignals) goes one step further: pass `"label" to values` pairs and it
traces them against a shared x with the [`signalPalette`](visualization.md#plotly-kt--signalpalette), optionally min-max normalized and with
dashed reference marks, then displays the plot into a channel of a live `Box` — it is already on
screen when it returns, so do not display it again.

[`toHtml`](visualization.md#plotly-kt--tohtml) renders a `Plot` into an HTML fragment via [`PlotlyIntegration`](visualization.md#plotly-kt-plotlyintegration). That fragment calls
`Plotly.react` in the browser, so the page has to have the Plotly library loaded already;
without it the fragment logs to the console and draws nothing.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/plotly.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/visualization/plotly/)

**Used in:** [Subharmonic Synthesis: an Octave Below](../subharmonic_sound.md), [Values over time: interpolants & keyframes](../interpolants_examples.md), [Motifs, Discords and Contrast: the Matrix Profile](../matrix_profile.md)

### PlotlyIntegration { #plotly-kt-plotlyintegration }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">public</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">PlotlyIntegration</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">PlotlyRenderer</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/visualization/plotly/#L503)

The `PlotlyRenderer` behind [`toHtml`](visualization.md#plotly-kt--tohtml): it emits a bare `div` plus a `Plotly.react` call against it, rather than the self-contained page plotly-kt's own renderers produce. That is what makes the output embeddable in a box output or a docs page that already loads Plotly.

The result is wrapped in a single enclosing div; the same "Plotly must already be loaded" caveat applies as for [`toHtml`](visualization.md#plotly-kt--tohtml). |

## someSkiko.kt { #someskiko-kt }

Drawing [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline)s into a box's output as SVG: [`Box.lines`](visualization.md#someskiko-kt--lines) and [`Box.l`](visualization.md#someskiko-kt--l) display them, [`linesToHTML`](visualization.md#someskiko-kt--linestohtml)
and [`drawToSVG`](visualization.md#someskiko-kt--drawtosvg) return the markup, and [`outputTo`](visualization.md#someskiko-kt--outputto) draws one line onto a Skia `Canvas`.

Lines carrying [`FLine.onClick`](graphics.md#standarddrawing-kt--onclick) or [`FLine.hoverColor`](graphics.md#standarddrawing-kt--hovercolor) are drawn as interactive SVG with click
callbacks; everything else goes through Skia's SVG canvas.

## tables.kt { #tables-kt }

Tabular output — the structure, and the one renderer for it.

[`Table`](visualization.md#tables-kt-table) is the counterpart of `showSignals` for data that is rows and columns rather than a
signal: build it, hand it to [`Box.showTable`](visualization.md#tables-kt--showtable) (or just let a box's last expression be one), and it
arrives on screen in the repo's output style. It implements [`ToHTML`](visualization.md#valuevisualizer-kt-tohtml), so `ValueVisualizer`
dispatches it ahead of everything else — `display(channel, table)`, `table.h`, and a returned
`Table` all render through [`Table.toHTML`](visualization.md#tables-kt--table--tohtml) with no extra wiring.

Why this exists: a box that wants a table has, until now, hand-rolled
`<table style='border-collapse:collapse…'>` with its own font stack, paddings and greys. A dozen
files under `src/` do exactly that and no two agree, which is a lot of markup standing between a
reader and what the box is actually saying.

The part that is not just formatting is [`Table.expect`](visualization.md#tables-kt--table--expect). A table in a doc or a live box usually
carries a *claim* — "every builder advanced one frame per pump", "no residual exceeds 1e-6" — and
a reader is otherwise asked to verify it by scanning cells. State the claim and the cells that
break it colour themselves, the footnote says how many did, and [`Table.deviations`](visualization.md#tables-kt--table--deviations) hands the same
list back to a test. That is the difference between showing a grid and showing an assertion you
can watch fail.

Trust model, same as the rest of value display: text produced by default formatting is escaped;
a string returned from a [`Table.format`](visualization.md#tables-kt--table--format) lambda is trusted HTML and inserted as-is.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/ui/visualization/tables.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/visualization/tables/)

**Used in:** [Frames and the animation loop](../animation_time_model.md), [How completions are ranked](../completion_ranking.md), [DataFrames in a Box](../dataframe.md)

### CellRole { #tables-kt-cellrole }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">CellRole</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">cssClass</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">cssVar</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/visualization/tables/#L94)

The semantic colour roles, shared with `markdown()`'s `{role:text}` spans — same six names, same `field-md-*` classes, so the same `--field-*` design token backs both. A cell that means "good" and a markdown span that means "good" are therefore the same colour by construction, and neither spells a hex literal.

Constants: `ACCENT`, `MUTED`, `DIM`, `OK`, `WARN`, `BAD`.

## visualizers.kt { #visualizers-kt }

Grouped controls whose value is more than one number: multisliders, matrices, range sliders,
menus and recorded gestures.

They are named after the Max/MSP objects they borrow from:
`multislider` ([`multiSlider`](visualization.md#visualizers-kt--multislider)), `matrixctrl` ([`matrix`](visualization.md#visualizers-kt--matrix)), `rslider` ([`rangeSlider`](visualization.md#visualizers-kt--rangeslider)) and `umenu`
([`menu`](visualization.md#visualizers-kt--menu)). All four travel the same way — the whole value as a list of doubles in one
`array-update` message (`ArrayControlUpdate`) — and are cached as comma-separated text in
`ControllerControl.text`, so a rerun restores them like any other grouped control. The pointer
handling is `src/commonMain/resources/arrayControls.js`.

The multislider, matrix and range slider also have a **playhead**: a position the box writes and
the person only sees. It is pushed like a meter reading ([`MeterHandle`](visualization.md#outputs-kt-meterhandle): rate-limited, in memory,
never cached, never calling back), so a sequencer can drive it from its clock every tick.

[`gesture`](visualization.md#visualizers-kt--gesture) records a pointer path as a looping take ([`GestureHandle`](visualization.md#visualizers-kt-gesturehandle)); [`ArcRange`](visualization.md#visualizers-kt-arcrange) and
[`arcContains`](visualization.md#visualizers-kt--arccontains) answer range questions on a circular dial.

### ArcRange { #visualizers-kt-arcrange }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">ArcRange</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">start</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">endInclusive</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ClosedFloatingPointRange</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/visualization/visualizers/#L494)

An interval on a circle, as a polar [`rangeSlider`](visualization.md#visualizers-kt--rangeslider) reports it: clockwise from `start` to `endInclusive`, wrapping through the top when `start > endInclusive`. `value in arc` and [`isEmpty`](visualization.md#visualizers-kt--arcrange--isempty) follow the arc, where an ordinary `1700.0..400.0` would read as empty.

### PenSample { #visualizers-kt-pensample }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">PenSample</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">t</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">pressure</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">NaN</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">tiltX</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">tiltY</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">twist</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/ui/visualization/visualizers/#L678)

One sample of a [`gesture`](visualization.md#visualizers-kt--gesture) take with what the pointer reported besides its position, as the browser's `PointerEvent` gives it: [`pressure`](visualization.md#visualizers-kt--pensample--pressure) 0 to 1 (a mouse with a button down reports 0.5), `tiltX` and `tiltY` the pen's lean in degrees toward +x (right) and toward the user (down the screen), -90 to 90, and `twist` its turn about its own axis, 0 to 359 degrees. A take recorded without `pen` has `NaN` pressure and no tilt or twist.
